builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Can We Make an LLM Dumber, or Is It Just Playing Dumb? An Empirical Study of Believable Performance Throttling
summary: This method replaces prompting, temperature scaling, and weight noise for deliberately reducing model performance to a target benchmark score. It requires training a LoRA adapter with weak-teacher data, adding training cost and deployment complexity. It can fail by converging to an answer-token attractor on multiple choice (up to 97% of new errors on one letter), transferring poorly across benchmarks (14.2-point error), and producing detectable error patterns despite local plausibility.
rationale: This technique addresses deliberate capability throttling for benchmark calibration research rather than a production need for constrained infrastructure, and its failure modes (attractor collapse, poor cross-benchmark transfer) make it unsuitable for adoption without further validation.
technique: Weak-teacher LoRA for calibrated performance reduction

claims.statement: This method replaces prompting, temperature scaling, and weight noise for deliberately reducing model performance to a target benchmark score. It requires training a LoRA adapter with weak-teacher data, adding training cost and deployment complexity. It can fail by converging to an answer-token attractor on multiple choice (up to 97% of new errors on one letter), transferring poorly across benchmarks (14.2-point error), and producing detectable error patterns despite local plausibility.

A weak-teacher LoRA dial reaches unseen target performance levels on reasoning tasks with a 1.9-point held-out calibration error, while logit interventions recover 52-59% of lost accuracy by correcting a dominant near-constant shift in multiple-choice settings.
